content:
Two conflicting reports appeared yesterday about next year's 20th anniversary iPhone, which is said to embody Apple's long-term vision of "a slab of glass".

We've already seen several inconsistent reports before, but yesterday's divergence was the most pronounced one so far……

What we know so far

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive has often spoken of his long-term vision of wanting the iPhone to eventually become "a slab of glass". The company is generally believed to have retained this vision after Ive's departure.

Although Apple generally doesn't make a big deal of celebrating product anniversaries, the industry consensus is that they want to get as close to this vision as possible before the iPhone's 20th anniversary. This could include embedding Face ID technology beneath the display, and even hiding the front camera under the screen as well.

However, we've already seen conflicting reports about what this will actually entail. Initially, some thought this would be a standalone model similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but more recent reports have suggested the design will be applied to next year's iPhone Pro lineup.

In sequential order, that would be the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple may also want to skip that numbering to celebrate the anniversary and call it the iPhone 20 directly.

Yesterday's conflicting reports

Yesterday, an analyst claimed Apple had abandoned the idea of an all-glass iPhone next year, adding to the confusion.

However, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman immediately pushed back on that claim.

The most likely reality

The key point here is that Apple's vision for the iPhone doesn't have a single endpoint. Whatever they plan for next year will only be one or several steps towards the sci-fi vision of "a slab of glass".

The question isn't whether this milestone can be reached next year, but how far Apple will go towards the vision. But whether it's one step or several, it certainly won't be the final step in iPhone design evolution.

In fact, Gurman says Apple has already taken a step back, dialling back somewhat from what they had originally hoped to achieve next year.

It's quite possible that the Jefferies analyst heard the same news, but only received it more recently, and thus interpreted it as the plan being completely abandoned.

My own expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap forward — on the order of magnitude of the iPhone X launch — but with more development still to come in subsequent years. For me, the big question is whether the leap for the 2027 iPhone will be large enough to require Apple to employ some special branding strategy, such as labelling it a 20th Anniversary Edition (which I think is unlikely), using some other special name, or skipping a generation to call it the iPhone 20 directly.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments.
